content: 1. The third edition of the Guidelines for Drinking-Water Quality, Volume 1: Recommendations was accessed on March 14, 2023, via the World Health Organization's (WHO) institutional repository. 2. The Global Status Report on Water Safety Plans provides a comprehensive review of proactive risk assessment and management practices to ensure the safety of drinking water. This document was accessed on March 14, 2023. 3. A field guide titled Improving Small Drinking-Water Supplies: Water Safety Planning for Rural Communities was published by the WHO Regional Office for Europe in Copenhagen. It offers practical guidance for rural communities and was accessed on March 14, 2023. 4. The WHO document Water Safety Planning for Small Community Water Supplies provides step-by-step risk management guidance for drinking-water supplies in small communities. This resource was accessed on March 14, 2023. 5. The thematic report Integrating Water Quality Testing into Household Surveys focuses on drinking water and was accessed on March 14, 2023. 6. The second edition of the Water and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement Tool (WASH FIT) is a practical guide for improving the quality of care through water, sanitation, and hygiene in healthcare facilities. Published by WHO in 2022, it was accessed on March 14, 2023. 7. The WHO publication Water Safety in Buildings addresses water safety management in building systems and was accessed on March 14, 2023. 8. The report Progress on Household Drinking Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene 2000–2022: Special Focus on Gender was accessed on March 14, 2023, and highlights global progress in these areas with a gender-specific lens. 9. A practical guide for auditing water safety plans, published by WHO, was accessed on August 15, 2023. 10. The WHO's Guidelines for Drinking-Water Quality: Small Water Supplies provides additional reading materials to support the guidance presented in Chapters 2 through 6 of the publication. These resources are not exhaustive but aim to elaborate on key topics. 11. Chapter 2 of the guidelines focuses on assessing the enabling environment, including costing and financing of small-scale water supply and sanitation services. Relevant resources include WHO publications and reports from organizations like the World Bank and OECD. 12. Chapter 3 emphasizes health-based regulations, including the development of drinking-water quality standards and regulations, particularly for resource-limited countries. WHO provides general guidance and technical resources to support these efforts. 13. Chapter 4 discusses water safety planning, offering tools and resources for equitable and climate-resilient water safety plans. It also includes guidance for small drinking-water supplies and rural communities. 14. Chapter 5 addresses surveillance, including practical guides for auditing water safety plans and strengthening drinking-water surveillance using risk-based approaches. WHO provides detailed guidance and case studies. 15. Chapter 6 focuses on improving data use for decision-making in water and sanitation. It highlights the importance of bridging technical expertise with real-world decision-making processes and includes resources from organizations like the World Bank and WaterAid. 16. The annex of the guidelines outlines the approach to content development and declarations of interest. It details the process of updating the WHO's 1997 guidelines, including expert meetings, working group recommendations, and global peer reviews. 17. The updated guidelines align with the framework for safe drinking water, emphasizing water safety planning. They incorporate the latest evidence base and good practice guidance, particularly for small drinking-water supplies. 18. WHO conducted a global survey in 2020 to develop tailored guidance for small water supplies. The draft publication underwent global peer review in 2022, with feedback from experts and practitioners across 24 countries. 19. All working group members and expert meeting attendees submitted declarations of interest to WHO to ensure objectivity and independence in the development of the guidelines. WHO reviewed these declarations and found no conflicts of interest. 20. The guidelines include references to key WHO publications, such as the second edition of Surveillance and Control of Community Supplies and supporting tools like sanitary inspection packages. These resources were accessed in 2023 and 2024, respectively.
